query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: At elevated temperatures under simultaneous mechanical wear and corrosive attack, the inherent lamellar (eutectic) microstructure of the multi‐phase high‐entropy alloy promotes selective oxidation at the phase boundaries (between the softer, Al–Ni–rich phase and the harder, B2 or FCC phase). This localized oxidation weakens the interfacial bonding, thereby accelerating both corrosion (by pitting and preferential dissolution) and wear (by facilitating spallation and removal of protective oxide scales).
generation.material_initial_state: A multi‐phase eutectic high‐entropy alloy (e.g., an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA) that has a fine, alternating lamellar microstructure consisting of a softer phase (rich in Al and Ni) and a harder phase (e.g., B2/FCC) as produced by casting or powder metallurgy (SPS).
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to simultaneous sliding wear (e.g., a reciprocating wear test with defined load and speed) and a corrosive environment (such as a chloride-containing acidic solution) at elevated temperatures (300–900 °C).
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures sufficient to accelerate diffusion (e.g., 600–900 °C), a corrosive medium (e.g., chloride–sulfuric acid solution) that challenges the passive films, and controlled mechanical loading mimicking sliding wear; tests should be conducted under atmospheres similar to service conditions where both oxidation and mechanical abrasion are active.
generation.structural_mediator: The finely spaced, alternating phases (lamellae) create numerous phase boundaries that are inherently susceptible to differential oxidation. These boundaries act as weak links where the softer phase oxidizes and corrodes preferentially, which in turn compromises the integrity of the overall microstructure under wear.
generation.mechanism: Elevated temperature accelerates defect diffusion and polarization at the phase interfaces. The softer (Al–Ni–rich) phase forms transient protective oxides that are mechanically removed by wear, exposing fresh material that then undergoes localized corrosion. This cycle at the phase boundaries leads to interfacial debonding and spallation, thus coupling and accelerating both degradation modes.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline sample (either a single-phase homogenized alloy or the same alloy under only corrosion or wear alone), the eutectic HEA should exhibit increased overall degradation: deeper wear tracks with lower friction stability due to repeated oxide spallation, and higher localized corrosion rates (evidenced by pitting preferentially at phase boundaries), leading to a higher mass loss.
generation.baseline: A matched alloy sample either processed to achieve a homogeneous (single-phase) microstructure or subjected solely to corrosion without an imposed wear cycle. Under equivalent temperature and environmental conditions, the baseline is expected to show lower degradation because the absence of distinct phase boundaries minimizes differential oxidation and the mechanical removal of protective scales.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for multi‐phase eutectic high‐entropy alloys with distinct alternating phases and well‐defined phase boundaries under conditions where temperature, mechanical load, and corrosive environment interact. The hypothesis may not apply if the oxide layer formed is exceptionally stable or if the microstructure is homogenized to a single solid solution.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence supports differential oxidation at phase interfaces, the quantitative contributions of oxidation-driven softening versus mechanical removal (wear) remain uncertain. Additionally, precise kinetic parameters for oxide formation and spallation under combined stress conditions need further experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (1) the eutectic HEA with its inherent lamellar microstructure and (2) a homogenized, single-phase variant of the same alloy. Subject both sets to identical simultaneous wear and corrosion tests at a fixed elevated temperature (e.g., 800 °C) in a controlled chloride-containing acidic solution. Monitor and compare the degradation behavior using wear track profiling, mass loss measurements, and localized electrochemical (pitting) assessments.
measurements: Wear depth and friction coefficient over time
Electrochemical corrosion rates (e.g., via potentiodynamic measurements)
Microscopic (SEM/EDS) analysis of the worn/corroded surfaces to evaluate phase-boundary degradation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the eutectic (lamellar) HEA does not show significantly more localized degradation at phase boundaries—as evidenced by comparable wear depths, friction behavior, and corrosion rates relative to the homogenized single-phase sample—or if degradation patterns are uniform rather than focused at interfaces, then the hypothesis that selective interfacial oxidation drives accelerated coupled wear–corrosion is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: ABSTRACTThe ongoing demand for high‐thrust turbine engines necessitates the advance of next‐generation structural materials capable of withstanding higher temperatures. Commercial MCrAlY alloy, used as bond coats crucial for thermal barrier coating (TBC) systems, face a fundamental temperature ceiling of ∼1100 °C due to accelerated oxidation and spallation. Here, we design a novel Y and Hf co‐doped NiCoCrAl‐type multi‐principal element alloy (MPEA) that achieves exceptional 1200 °C oxidation resistance primarily through lattice distortion‐induced diffusion suppression. Compared with typical NiCoCrAlY alloy, the MPEA exhibits 59% lower in thermally grown oxide (TGO) growth rate, as well as negligible TGO spallation after 500 h at 1200°C. This performance stems from a significantly refined eutectic structure enabling rapid formation of a protective Al2O3 scale during initial oxidation, coupled with lattice distortion that elevates vacancy formation energy and Al migration barriers within the Al‐depletion zone (ADZ), drastically reducing sustained diffusion rates. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Based on the above conclusions, the corrosion process of the EHEA in the test solution is schematically described in Figure 14. The passive films of few Al-Ni-rich phases are attacked by Cl− at lower temperature (Figure 14a2), and then occurs localized corrosion (Figure 14a3); while the passive films of Al-Ni-rich phases are damaged (Figure 14b2), and more Al-Ni-rich phases are dissolved at higher temperature (Figure 14b3). Metastable pits are preferentially created on the grain boundary or B2 phase. Pitting is enhanced by the effect of polarization. Due to autocatalysis by the caustic ions, the metastable pits gradually grow in the pitting corrosion area or the selective dissolution region. Moreover, the size of the selective dissolution region increases with temperature, and pitting occurs on the surface at various temperatures.
